title: Trump Administration Weighs $100,000 Fee on Foreign Student Work Program
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security is considering a $100,000 price tag on Optional Practical Training, the post-graduation work program used by more than 294,000 international students annually.
body:
• The Trump administration is considering a $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT), the program that lets international graduates work in the US for one to three years after completing their degrees.
  • The move follows a failed attempt to impose a similar $100,000 fee on H-1B visa sponsorships, which was blocked by federal courts in July 2026.
  • More than 294,000 students used OPT in 2024-25, with Indians comprising 40% of the total — making them by far the most affected group.
  • Legal experts say the fee would face "serious legal obstacles," and it remains unclear whether students, employers, or universities would bear the cost.

The Trump administration is considering attaching a $100,000 fee to the Optional Practical Training program, the post-graduation work authorization that serves as a critical bridge between an F-1 student visa and long-term employment in the United States, according to a Wall Street Journal report.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed that the fee is under discussion but cautioned that "no policy should be considered final until it is formally announced." The proposal does not specify whether students, employers, or universities would be required to pay.

A Pivot After H-1B Fee Blocked in Court

The OPT fee proposal arrives after the administration's earlier attempt to impose a $100,000 fee on H-1B visa sponsorships hit a wall. President Trump signed a proclamation in September 2025 requiring employers to pay $100,000 per H-1B petition — a massive jump from the existing fees of roughly $3,000. Federal courts blocked enforcement, and a Boston appeals court rejected the administration's appeal on July 24, 2026.

By targeting OPT instead, the administration could achieve a similar outcome: dramatically reducing the number of foreign graduates who transition from student visas to US employment. OPT currently allows graduates with bachelor's degrees up to 12 months of work authorization, with STEM graduates eligible for a 24-month extension — a total of three years that often serves as a runway to H-1B sponsorship.

Indian Students Stand to Lose the Most

Indians account for nearly one-third of all international students in the US. In 2025, 40% of Indian students in the country were on OPT — nearly double the proportion from the previous year — making them the community most exposed to the proposed fee.

"The charge would exceed the first-year gross salary of most STEM master's graduates. No Indian lender underwrites a loan against a debt the borrower must pay before earning anything."

— Rajiv S. Khanna, Managing Attorney, Immigration.com

For most Indian families, a US degree already requires significant loans. Adding a $100,000 fee on top of tuition — which can exceed $50,000 per year at many universities — would upend the financial calculus that has driven Indian enrollment in American institutions for decades.

Sanjay Laul, founder of MSM Unify, said roughly 419,000 international graduates use OPT each year, disproportionately in STEM fields, contributing an estimated $43 billion to the US economy and supporting more than 355,000 American jobs.

Brain Drain and University Revenue at Risk

A Chronicle of Higher Education survey found that eight in ten international students would not choose to study in the US if they could not access OPT. With six in ten US colleges already reporting a decline in international applications due to ongoing policy uncertainty, the fee could accelerate a broader retreat.

The stakes are particularly high for doctoral programs. In 2023, international students on F-1 visas earned 34% of all PhDs awarded by US institutions — nearly half of those went to Chinese or Indian students. A 2025 Silicon Valley Index report found that 66% of technology workers in the region are foreign-born.

Green Card Bond Also Under Consideration

The OPT fee is not the only measure on the table. State Department officials are also weighing a $100,000 bond on green card applications filed from outside the US, redeemable only after the applicant moves to the country and becomes a citizen.

Legal Challenges Expected

Immigration attorneys widely expect litigation if the fee moves forward. The H-1B fee has already been declared unlawful, and legal experts have questioned the administration's authority to impose a fee of this magnitude on OPT.

Khanna advised Indian students and families to "plan on the assumption that American immigration policy will remain unstable through at least 2027," and to evaluate post-study work options across multiple countries rather than betting exclusively on the US.

New OPT rules are separately slated for introduction in February 2027, with the government indicating it will address "fraud and national security concerns" and "protect US workers from being displaced by foreign nationals."
